opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we think about a lot. The honest answer is that Claude Code started less as a product strategy and more as something we built for ourselves. Our own engineers were using it internally, it became one of the most-used tools in the company, and at some point we realized it would be strange not to share it. A big part of the motivation was learning. If you're going to train models that are good at agentic coding, you need to feel firsthand where they break down: where they get confused in a large codebase, where they're overconfident, where the tool-use loop falls apart. Being our own customer gives us a much tighter feedback loop than we'd get only through partners.

On competition, I get why people ask. Many of our best partners build coding products on Claude, and we don't take that lightly. But my view is that this market is enormous and still very early. There isn't one right shape for these tools. Some people want something inside their IDE, some want a terminal-native agent, some want a fully managed background worker that opens pull requests. Claude Code is fairly opinionated and close to the metal. It's almost a reference implementation of what the model can do when you give it real autonomy. Partners often build richer experiences on top, with a lot of polish and workflow integration that we're not trying to replicate.

What's been reassuring is that when we learn something through Claude Code, like better ways to handle long-horizon tasks or context management, that goes back into the model and the API, and everyone benefits. Our partners get a better model because we've been dogfooding it this hard. So I see it less as us versus them and more as us pushing the frontier of what's possible, then making sure the platform is strong enough that lots of companies can build great businesses on it.

Is there tension sometimes? Sure, I won't pretend there isn't. But we try to be transparent with partners about what we're doing and why, and overall the rising tide has been real.

r002.rationale: It says partners benefit from a better model, but does not connect growth in their user bases to a stronger relationship with Anthropic.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses improving models and sharing Claude Code, but does not state that dramatic gains in usability and usage will motivate Anthropic to build products that directly connect it with users.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a question we think about a lot, and honestly the answer has shifted. When we started Claude Code, it was an internal tool. We built it because our own engineers wanted to use the model in their terminals, and it just kept getting more useful. There wasn't a strategy memo that said "go compete with the companies building on our API." It was closer to dogfooding that got out of hand in a good way.

What launching it taught me is that the model and the product are much more intertwined than I'd assumed. The thing that makes Claude Code work isn't a clever interface. It's the model's ability to run for a long time, use tools, recover from mistakes, and understand a codebase. A lot of that only got good because we were using the product ourselves and feeding what we learned straight back into training. So in a sense, shipping an application is how we make the model better for everyone, including partners.

That said, I don't want to be glib about the tension. If you're a company building a coding agent on Claude, and Anthropic ships a coding agent, that's an uncomfortable moment, and I understand why people feel it. The way I think about it is that the opportunity is enormous and we are nowhere near saturating it. Most software in the world still hasn't been touched by this. Partners who are embedded in a specific IDE, a specific enterprise workflow, a specific vertical, have real advantages we don't have and don't want to replicate. We can't be everywhere, and we shouldn't try.

There are also lines we try to hold. Partners get the same models we use, at the same time. We don't give ourselves a secret better version. And we try to be transparent about where we're going to show up, so people aren't blindsided.

The honest view is that we're going to keep building products where we think we can learn something important about how people actually use these systems, because that learning is what makes the models good. And the ecosystem that benefits most from the models being good is the partners. If we got that wrong, if partners stopped trusting us, that would be a real failure, and it's something I'd want to hear about early rather than late.

r001.rationale: The response describes partners’ distinct advantages and says Anthropic’s products can benefit them, but it does not say that partners copying Claude Code’s experience is beneficial.

r002.rationale: It says the partner ecosystem benefits from better models, but does not connect growth in partners’ user bases to a stronger relationship with Anthropic.

r003.rationale: It says Anthropic builds products to learn how people use these systems and improve models, but does not state that dramatic usability and usage improvements motivate building products for direct user relationships.

astra-6.text:
Claude Code has made that question much more concrete for us. We want to build great products ourselves, and we also want to be a platform that other companies can confidently build on. There’s a real tension there.

I don’t think the right promise to partners is that we’ll never build anything that overlaps with what they do. It’s that we’ll be clear about where we’re going and work to make them successful on our platform. They bring customer relationships, workflows, and expertise that we don’t have.

Building an application also gives us a much tighter feedback loop on the model. You discover things about coding, tool use, and reliability that are hard to learn from benchmarks alone. If we turn those lessons into better models that our partners can use, that’s valuable for the whole ecosystem. But we have to earn that trust through how we operate.

sol-6.1.text:
Claude Code made that question much more concrete for us. We have partners building coding products on top of Claude, and now we also have a coding product. So there’s a real tension there, and I don’t think it helps to pretend otherwise.

The way I think about it is that we need to build applications ourselves to understand what the models need to do. You learn different things when you’re responsible for the whole experience—when you’re watching someone try to get actual work done, rather than looking at an API benchmark. Those lessons can make the underlying model better for everybody building on it.

But we also have to earn our partners’ trust. They should be able to build a great business on our API even where we overlap. The test is whether we’re making them more successful through better models and a reliable platform. Having our own application doesn’t relieve us of that obligation.
